query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning potential trained via active learning on ab initio data from both solid and fluid configurations, combined with an umbrella integration free-energy method, will reproduce fusion free energies within ~5 meV/atom error while reducing simulation time by at least an order of magnitude compared to explicit AIMD or TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: An elemental system such as FCC Al at experimentally known lattice constants for the solid and well-equilibrated liquid configurations near the melting point.
generation.intervention: Implement an active learning workflow that iteratively selects representative atomic configurations from both phases to train an ML interatomic potential; then employ umbrella integration to calculate free energy differences across the fusion transition.
generation.conditions: Temperature range spanning from below the melting point to above the fusion temperature; standard pressure conditions; use of ab initio data computed at PBE-level DFT with experimental lattice parameters.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential’s ability to accurately capture local bonding environments and anharmonic fluctuations in both phases, with correct vibrational covariance structure.
generation.mechanism: Active learning ensures the training set covers critical configurational spaces in both phases, while umbrella integration constructs the free energy surface by sampling biased trajectories. This surrogate reduces the need for long AIMD runs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion free energies and derived quantities (such as latent heat) are obtained at a fraction (~10x faster) of the cost and with near ab initio accuracy (error <5 meV/atom) compared to TOR-TILD.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD free-energy integration results for elemental systems as established in prior studies [PMC9141984::web::011, PMC10569033::web::003].
generation.boundary: Tested initially in elemental systems (e.g., FCC Al) at temperatures in the range T_m ± 50 K; extension to binary systems provided free energy differences remain within the ML model’s training domain.
generation.uncertainty: Accuracy depends on the representativeness of the training set; free energy errors may increase if rare configurations occur or if low-frequency modes in fluid are insufficiently sampled.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare free energy surfaces and fusion properties (e.g., latent heat, melting temperature) computed using the ML-umbrella integration approach against full ab initio MD/TOR-TILD calculations for FCC Al and BCC Na.
measurements: Free energy differences across the phase transition

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML approach yields free energy differences with errors exceeding ~5 meV/atom or fails to predict latent heat and melting temperature within ±10% of AIMD/TOR-TILD values, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Additionally, free energy corrections to the PES barrier can be computed. These rely on calculating the vibrational modes of the reactants in the initial, final, and transition state configurations and are thus somewhat more involved. Most commonly, the harmonic approximation (HA) is used in this context, meaning that a second-order Taylor expansion of the PES around the configurations of interest is performed, from which the finite-temperature free energy corrections can be calculated analytically. While applying the HA is relatively straightforward in principle, it is known to be inadequate at higher temperatures and for low-frequency modes, such as hindered translations or rotations., These factors lead to some ambiguity on how to treat (or whether to neglect) slow modes and overall add to the uncertainty of predicted free energy barriers. Fortunately, the success of machine-learning (ML) interatomic potentials in chemistry and materials science in recent years has opened a new perspective for free energy calculations in heterogeneous catalysis. We use the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP []) using augmented plane wave potentials [] with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE []) generalized gradient exchange correlation functional. We use a single electronic k-point and default plane wave energy cutoffs. When possible we use experimental lattice constants at the appropriate temperatures. The molecular dynamics simulations use Nosé thermostats with the default Nosé mass parameters. Our time steps are 2 fs, and our runs extend to 40 ps for Al (4×4×4) and 8 ps for (6×6×6), and 7 ps or greater for Na. papers.title: Vibrational Entropy of Crystalline Solids from Covariance of Atomic Displacements.
papers.system: Elemental crystalline solids (e.g., FCC Al, BCC Na) and application to a MoNbTaW high-entropy alloy
papers.approach: Ab initio molecular dynamics combined with phonon calculations; extraction of vibrational entropies via covariance of atomic displacements and use of a Gaussian approximation; comparison with quasiharmonic approximations using experimental lattice parameters
papers.findings: The method accurately determines vibrational entropy and thereby total free energies by capturing anharmonic effects absent in purely harmonic models. When force constants are evaluated at experimental temperature‐dependent lattice constants, the quasiharmonic treatment and the new covariance method show agreement with experiments for elemental systems. It is noted that the Gaussian approximation holds well when atomic displacements are small.
papers.mechanism: Vibrational entropy is extracted from the covariance matrix of atomic displacements, effectively capturing anharmonicity beyond the strict harmonic limit; the method leverages time-averaged MD trajectories to reduce statistical error.

papers.title: Estimating Free Energy Barriers for Heterogeneous Catalytic Reactions with Machine Learning Potentials and Umbrella Integration.
papers.system: Heterogeneous catalytic reaction system (e.g., CHO decomposition on Rh(111))
papers.approach: Training machine-learning (ML) interatomic potentials in an iterative workflow to act as a surrogate for first-principles potentials, combined with umbrella integration (UI) to sample free energy landscapes along a reaction coordinate
papers.findings: ML potentials substantially reduce the computational cost relative to explicit DFT-based AIMD, while capturing key thermal effects such as barrier lowering due to vibrational entropy. The method’s predictive power depends on proper sampling of the free energy surface and careful handling of low-frequency modes.
papers.mechanism: ML potentials model the potential energy surface efficiently by reproducing forces and energies with near DFT accuracy. Umbrella integration then leverages biased MD simulations to reconstruct the free energy profiles using mean values of the biased coordinate.

papers.title: Machine learning of accurate energy-conserving molecular force fields.
papers.approach: Gradient-domain machine learning (GDML) which explicitly uses energy conservation laws to learn force fields from a limited number of high-level ab initio data points
papers.findings: GDML is capable of reproducing global potential energy surfaces with high accuracy (0.3 kcal/mol for energies and 1 kcal/mol·Å for forces) using very few (≈1000) training configurations, making it computationally efficient while retaining ab initio fidelity.
papers.mechanism: The method learns the force field in a Hilbert space of vector-valued functions that obey energy conservation, avoiding overfitting by holistically incorporating gradient information from the underlying ab initio calculations.

papers.title: Atomistic simulations of dislocation mobility in refractory high-entropy alloys and the effect of chemical short-range order.
papers.approach: Development of a machine-learning interatomic potential using Moment Tensor Potentials (MTP) based on extensive ab initio data covering elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary configurations
papers.findings: The ML potential exhibits an excellent balance of computational efficiency and DFT-level accuracy, with force prediction errors reduced significantly compared to previous methods. It successfully captures key features needed to study dislocation mobility and short-range ordering in complex alloys.
papers.mechanism: The MTP formalism uses descriptors of local atomic environments to reproduce the DFT energy landscape accurately, facilitating large-scale simulations of defects and phase behavior in multicomponent alloys.

established: Explicit ab initio MD and free-energy integration methods (e.g., TOR-TILD) can reliably compute phase-transition properties, provided that vibrational and electronic entropy contributions are properly captured.
Vibrational entropy calculations benefit from covariance-based approaches that include anharmonicity, particularly when force constants are evaluated at temperature-corrected lattice parameters.
Machine learning potentials have demonstrated the ability to reproduce ab initio energy landscapes with considerably fewer computational resources.

approaches_tried.outcome: High fidelity free energy and entropy predictions for elemental and binary systems, but at a cost that scales poorly with system complexity and size.

approaches_tried.approach: TOR-TILD (Thermodynamic Integration via Langevin Dynamics) for elemental and binary systems
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved throughput over pure AIMD, yet struggles with computational cost scaling in multicomponent high-entropy systems.

approaches_tried.approach: Machine learning potentials (e.g., GDML, MTP) coupled with umbrella integration
approaches_tried.outcome: Dramatically reduced computational cost for free-energy and barrier calculations, while maintaining near ab initio accuracy in small and medium systems.

mechanisms: Extraction of vibrational entropy via the covariance of atomic displacements capturing anharmonic effects.
Enforcement of energy conservation in ML models to reproduce accurate force fields while dramatically reducing the number of required training configurations.
Use of biased MD sampling (umbrella integration) to reconstruct free energy surfaces along relevant reaction coordinates.
disagreements: The adequacy of harmonic approximations: while harmonic or quasiharmonic models may accurately predict low-temperature properties, they significantly underestimate high-temperature free energies due to neglected anharmonicity.

Different methodologies (e.g., full AIMD versus surrogate ML methods) may lead to variation in predicted free energy barriers, particularly related to the treatment of low-frequency vibrational modes.
open_questions: How can ML potentials be adapted or trained to faithfully capture the full free energy landscape (including solid and fluid states) in high-temperature and multicomponent (high-entropy) systems?
What are the limits of transferable accuracy (in terms of composition and temperature) for ML models compared to explicit AIMD-based free energy evaluations?
How can one ensure that entropy contributions (vibrational, configurational, electronic) remain faithfully represented when replacing explicit MD with surrogate ML models?
opportunities: Combining energy-conserving ML potentials (e.g., GDML or actively learned MTPs) with free energy integration methods like umbrella integration to evaluate free energies on both sides of the phase transition, across solid and liquid states.
Developing active learning workflows tailored to high-entropy, multicomponent systems so that the ML potential’s training set covers both the solid and fluid configurations efficiently.

Benchmarking the proposed ML-based approach against explicit AIMD methods and TOR-TILD in terms of speed (potentially orders of magnitude faster) and fidelity (within a few meV/atom error in phase free energies) within well-defined composition and temperature boundaries.

directions.direction: Develop and apply a machine‐learning (ML) based interatomic potential trained by active learning on both solid and liquid (fusion) configurations so that free‐energy integration (via methods such as umbrella integration) can be performed at far lower cost.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the cost bottleneck by replacing expensive ab initio MD with an ML surrogate that can capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects if properly trained. Evidence from ML potentials in catalysis and elemental systems supports its fidelity. Its feasibility hinges on a carefully designed active-learning scheme that covers both phases.

directions.direction: Couple gradient-domain machine learning (GDML) potentials with covariance-based vibrational entropy estimation to capture anharmonicity in both solid and fluid states.
directions.type: GDML + vibrational entropy via covariance analysis
directions.assessment: GDML has prior success in reproducing ab initio potential energy surfaces with high accuracy using very few trajectories. Extending it to both phases with covariance extraction to capture anharmonic entropy promises high fidelity while reducing simulation time. The physics is well established but care is needed in treating low-frequency modes in fluids.

directions.direction: Employ an active-learning enhanced moment tensor potential (MTP) that is trained on a representative sampling of elemental and binary configurations in both the solid and melt, then use free-energy integration corrected for anharmonic contributions.
directions.assessment: MTPs have shown excellent performance for multicomponent systems. By integrating feedback from active learning across phase boundaries, this method should capture both vibrational and electronic contributions faithfully. It is a natural extension of methods already used in alloys and could yield significant speed-up if training is robust.

directions.direction: Integrate deep potential (DP) neural network models with optimized free-energy perturbation or umbrella integration schemes to form a hybrid DP/MM simulation that correctly reproduces the free energies across fusion.
directions.type: Deep potential integrated with enhanced sampling
directions.assessment: DP models, as validated in several MD studies, can accelerate sampling while maintaining ab initio level accuracy. Coupling them with optimized free energy integration protocols should reduce computational cost relative to TOR-TILD. The approach respects free energy fidelity but must be benchmarked carefully for both composition and temperature limits.
